name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,755

indicators.note: something thrown is tossed about and lands in disorder, so these letters are scattered
lying across something means spanning it, so one piece stretches over and around the other

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
I is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Someone lobs a pebble, maybe, over to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone perhaps' reads as one phrase, but 'perhaps' belongs to the wordplay: its seven letters are scrambled into SAPPH-RE with I placed across them to give SAPPHIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A sapphire is a precious gem, and gems are called stones in the jewellery trade.

blocks.note: SE is the postcode area for south-east London, so this Londoner is placed there
a toff is British slang for an upper-class person

explanation.surface: A quiz-style definition: what sets off a posh Londoner?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags whimsy: a posh person from south-east London, named by postcode then slang, is joined up and then split at a different point. A toff is British slang for a posh person.
explanation.definitionFit: To trigger something is to start it or make it go, as an alarm or explosion is started.

blocks.note: pent, as in pent-up, means confined
eco- is the prefix for environmentally friendly things
St is the usual abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A festival confined to a single street called Green Street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green Street' looks like an address, but the two words are separate pieces, green in its environmental sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Pentecost is the Christian feast celebrating the descent of the Holy Spirit, seven weeks after Easter.

clue.text: Rock and roll star losing head about the French/Scandinavian boy from Missouri

indicators.note: losing a head means the top is cut off, so the opening letter is dropped
about means around, so one piece is wrapped around another

blocks.note: Chuck Berry, the rock and roll pioneer, without his first letter
le is French for the
a Finn is a native of Finland

explanation.surface: A beheaded rock star, a French article and a Nordic boy tangled in one Missouri story.
explanation.walkthrough: Chuck Berry was a 1950s rock and roll pioneer; with his head gone his first name becomes a nickname, and the French article sits between first name and surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Huckleberry Finn is Mark Twain's young hero, who grows up in a small town on the Mississippi in Missouri.

indicators.note: in a down answer, heading north means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards
to welcome is to take in a guest, so one piece holds another inside it

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps
to link things is to join or unite them

explanation.surface: Railway engineers taking on a new northern rail link.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' and 'link' suggest railways, and 'northern' seems geographical; in a down clue, going north means writing upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A train is the group of attendants following an important person, which is exactly what a retinue is.

blocks.note: a band is a group of musicians
it is old slang for sex appeal

explanation.surface: Musicians make an appeal on behalf of the song Desperado.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Desperado look like a title, the Eagles song, but it is simply the definition. IT for appeal is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless outlaw, and a bandit is a robber of the same lawless kind.

clue.text: Lawyer for government agent nearly tore free

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and can fall into a new one

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A government agent almost ripped himself loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' looks like it trims a word, but it is fodder, all six letters used; 'for government' belongs to the definition rather than to the agent.
explanation.definitionFit: The Attorney General is the chief law officer who advises the government and represents it in court.

indicators.note: rising up in a down answer means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Christian Dior, the French fashion designer
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: The inventor of a robot was killed in a rebellion, a sci-fi plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In uprising' reads as the place of death, but it is the reversal signal: DIOR then D, written upwards, gives DROID.
explanation.definitionFit: Droid is a short form of android, a science-fiction robot, popularised by Star Wars.

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters
taken as written
being positive about something is being sure of it

explanation.surface: Advice to aim routinely for a positive number, like a maths or sales goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Positive value' looks like a single maths phrase; the definition is 'value' alone, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To value something highly is to cherish it, which is the verb sense of treasure.

blocks.note: taken as written
greed is one of the seven deadly sins

explanation.surface: Someone guiltily confesses that yes, it is a sin.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a confession; split the answer as A GREED, greed being one of the seven deadly sins.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying agreed is an interjection of assent, used in conversation exactly like saying yes or okay.

clue.text: Spur on to enter movement, against one's will

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: taken as written
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: Urging someone into a political movement they never wanted to join.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spur on' reads as one phrasal verb, but the definition is 'Spur' alone, and 'movement' is a bodily twitch, not a political cause.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonic is something that stimulates or invigorates, and a spur is likewise an incentive or stimulus.

clue.text: Near Truss, where balance can be tricky

blocks.note: near and tight both mean stingy with money
to truss is to tie up, as with rope

explanation.surface: Standing close to Liz Truss, the short-lived UK prime minister, is politically precarious.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital makes Truss the former prime minister, and the balance seems political or budgetary; both words are ordinary verbs and adjectives in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking a tightrope is the classic circus act demanding perfect balance on a stretched wire.

clue.text: Future partner accepting pitch for setter to work on assignment

indicators.note: taking one thing in exchange for another is a swap, so a letter is replaced by a new piece

blocks.note: a fiancé is someone engaged to marry
a ship that pitches lurches or reels
the crossword setter refers to themselves as I; this letter comes out

explanation.surface: A fiancée accepts a sales pitch so that the crossword setter can work on a commission.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is I, so REEL replaces the I in FIANCE. The clue slyly describes the setter's own job, done freelance for newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: To freelance is to take on paid jobs for various clients rather than being employed, working on assignment.

clue.text: Good to abandon crests for teacups etc.

indicators.note: abandoning something means leaving it behind, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good; this letter comes out
crests are ridges, hilltops, shown here without the G

explanation.surface: An odd instruction to give up heraldic crests in favour of teacups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teacups etc.' looks like crockery, but it means the spinning teacup ride at a fairground; RIDGES loses its G.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinning teacups are a classic funfair attraction, one example of the amusements called rides.

indicators.note: a cover goes over and around, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: cross and sore both mean annoyed
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A cross laid over a doctor's burial place.
explanation.walkthrough: Cross and grave together suggest a churchyard; cross is an adjective meaning angry, and grave an adjective meaning serious.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave as an adjective means serious and gloomy, the same mood that sombre describes.

clue.text: One who helps in theatre, being right next to doctor

indicators.note: next to means placed alongside, so pieces are joined end to end

blocks.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
esse is Latin for to be, used in English for existence or being
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: An assistant in the operating theatre stands right beside the surgeon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theatre' and 'doctor' together suggest surgery, but the theatre is the stage; ESSE is a Latin word for being that crosswords use often.
explanation.definitionFit: A dresser is the backstage assistant who helps actors into costumes during a stage production.

clue.text: I'll get loads round to destroy screens

indicators.note: turning round means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: to erode is to wear away and destroy gradually
vets as a verb means checks or screens candidates

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of getting plenty of rounds in, as if at a bar, before smashing television screens.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is written in the first person: the answer itself says it will get loads. ERODE VETS read backwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A stevedore is a dock worker whose job is loading and unloading cargo on ships.

indicators.note: fiddling with something means tinkering with it, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
to tax someone is to strain or try them

explanation.surface: A study of financial fiddling in the tax affairs of the DUP, Northern Ireland's Democratic Unionist Party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddling' and 'tax' together suggest fraud, but fiddling scrambles IN DUP and tax is a verb meaning to strain.
explanation.definitionFit: Punditry is expert commentary and opinion, the kind of analysis offered by television experts.

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so losing it means the middle letters are dropped

blocks.note: to articulate words is to utter them
the word with its middle two letters gone

explanation.surface: A rather eloquent woman who has become disheartened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite articulate' reads as 'fairly eloquent', but 'Quite' stands alone as the definition and 'articulate' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Quite in its stronger sense means completely, as in quite finished, which matches utterly.

indicators.note: to include something is to contain it, so the letters sit inside the words

blocks.note: sitting across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Farewells arranged so as to let the dog come too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poodle' seems to be a dog; in British usage it is a servile follower, famously said of a prime minister and a US president.
explanation.definitionFit: A poodle in British political slang is a fawning follower who always agrees, which describes a yes-man.

clue.text: Something from Farrow & Ball's ultimately put in tip, e.g. recycled

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept
recycled material is broken down and remade, so these letters are reformed
putting something in means inserting it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the last letter of the word
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A leftover tin of Farrow & Ball paint, the upmarket British brand, dumped at the rubbish tip for recycling.
explanation.walkthrough: Farrow & Ball looks like one brand name, but the ampersand separates them: a farrow is a litter of pigs.
explanation.definitionFit: A farrow is a litter of young pigs, so each piglet is one member produced from a farrow.

blocks.note: a and per both mean each, as in once a day
second-hand goods are used ones

explanation.walkthrough: 'A second-hand read' sounds like a used book; A as PER, as in 'ten pounds a head', is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: To peruse is to read through something, so perused works as the past tense of read.

blocks.note: a fine is a monetary penalty
RY is the abbreviation for railway, and railway lines are lines

explanation.surface: A schoolteacher's view that the best punishment is writing lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Lines look like the school punishment of copying a sentence out; here they are railway lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Your Sunday best means your smartest clothes, and finery is elaborate or showy clothing.

indicators.note: at last means at the very end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: a dish is an item of food
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Finally fetching the food trolley, as on a train or plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fetching' reads as going to get, but it is the adjective meaning attractive; dishy is British slang for good-looking.
explanation.definitionFit: Fetching means attractive, and dishy is informal British slang for a good-looking person.

indicators.note: outside means surrounding, so one piece is wrapped around the other

blocks.note: a scam is a trick or swindle
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A football move: trick the defender on the outside right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside right' is an old football position, but here 'outside' is the container signal and 'right' is just R.
explanation.definitionFit: Scram is a curt command to go away, and move is used the same way, as in get moving.

clue.text: Part of Africa still shortly to receive independence

indicators.note: shortly means cut short, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: serene means calm and still, here missing its last letter
to get something is to receive it
I is the abbreviation for independence or independent

explanation.surface: An African region still expecting to gain its independence soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' reads as 'soon', but it trims SERENE by one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti is a vast plain in Tanzania and Kenya, famous for its wildlife migrations.

indicators.note: something done in is wrecked and broken up, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, since tram lines are finished at their terminals, and the whole clue is also the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Terminals are the end stations where transport routes stop, so a tram line is done there.

clue.text: Horn played by head of early riser in the Alps

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the opening letter is kept
something played is performed in a new way, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: An alphorn played by a shepherd who gets up at dawn in the Alps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early riser' looks like one phrase, but 'early' supplies a letter and 'riser' belongs to the definition: a river rises at its source.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhône river has its source in the Rhône Glacier in the Swiss Alps before flowing into France.

clue.text: Want to tour Middle East with one who's local?

indicators.note: a tour goes all the way round a place, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: a yen is a longing or want
ME is the abbreviation for the Middle East
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Hoping to travel round the Middle East accompanied by a local guide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' does double duty on purpose: it gives the final I and also starts the definition. The question mark marks the local as local to the Middle East the clue itself mentions.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yemeni is a native of Yemen, a country in the Middle East, so a local of that region.

clue.text: Upset at rudely breaking marriage vows

definitions.note: a gerund phrase standing for the noun, the act of breaking vows

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone upset at a spouse brazenly breaking their wedding vows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rudely' looks like it describes the breaking, but it is fodder; 'Upset' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Adultery is infidelity by a married person, which breaks the promise of faithfulness made in the wedding vows.
